source.title: STELLAR: Scaling 3D Perception Large Models for Autonomous Driving
source.authors: Ying-Wei Li; Xin Huang; Yang Liu; Yang Fu; A. Zhu; Chen Song; Jun Yao; Anant Subramanian; Haoen Xiang; Weijing Shi; Yu-Liang Zou; Tom Hoddes; Zhaoqi Leng; Govind Thattai; D. Anguelov; Ming-Xing Tan

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in 3D perception and reports that its loss curves show diminishing returns rather than the strong log-linear trends reported for language models; it also describes a compute-allocation pattern favoring more data.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling losses in Figures 3–5 and downstream WOD performance in Table 6. Cited language-model scaling results are not treated as findings from this study. Other ablations are omitted because they do not bear on the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own model-, data- and compute-scaling sweeps of a multimodal 3D-perception transformer: up to 483M parameters, 51.2M driving examples and more than 10 ZettaFLOPs. It reports pretraining-loss curves (Figs 3–5) and downstream WOD detection versus model size (Table 6). This is a new setting (supervised and auto-labelled 3D detection) with results that bear on V5, V6 and V7. T3 fits better than T5: the paper is mainly a scaling study in a new domain, and its departure from LLM-like laws is a side observation, not a targeted argument against a version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors report that loss improves with model size, data and compute, but with diminishing returns rather than LLM-like log-linear laws. They attribute this to fixed-size non-transformer components, auto-label quality and driving-data redundancy. At fixed compute, more data is more efficient. Scaling gains transfer to WOD detection, and the 483M model sets a new WOD state of the art. They conclude that large-scale multimodal, multi-task training is a pivotal direction for perception.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales a multimodal 3D perception model trained on supervised and auto-labeled driving data, measuring detection losses and downstream detection performance rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy. Its compute comparisons are qualitative and do not fit an optimal parameter/token power law.
record.method_sensitivity: The model-scaling loss curves flatten more for larger datasets; the data-scaling curves show diminishing returns. The authors attribute curve distortion to fixed-size non-transformer components, auto-label quality, and redundancy in driving data.

fits_no_version.finding: The compute-efficient frontier is dominated by the largest dataset. At a fixed FLOP budget, a smaller model on more data beats a larger model on little data. This is shown only qualitatively, with no fitted allocation law.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In 3D-perception pretraining, compute-optimal allocation favours data over parameters.

record.problems: The scaling figures provide no numerical loss values, fit coefficients, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests in the text. The compute-optimal allocation result is qualitative and does not quantify an optimal scaling exponent.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported result was left out. Other ablations concern training recipe, modalities, temporal context, range, and distillation rather than the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling; no LM is trained.
No test of whether small-run fits predict much larger runs.
No fitted growth of optimal parameter or data count with compute. Only a qualitative frontier favouring the largest dataset is reported.
Width and depth are co-scaled; shape is never varied at a fixed parameter count.
Image/video generative models, repeated data, and fine-tuning or transfer scaling laws.
No fitted predictive mapping from scale or pretraining loss to downstream metrics; data-size effects downstream are only qualitative (Figs 7, 10).
Fitting method, parameter counting and schedule are not varied (the schedule is constant LR throughout).

missing.what: Rare-class scaling on an internal dataset: mAP +5.5% from 25M to 96M and +7.9% from 96M to 483M. On a rare/hard benchmark, 483M has 25% lower error than 96M.
Downstream L2 APH versus pretraining FLOPs.
Per-class Table 6 values (vehicle, pedestrian, cyclist) across 25M, 96M and 483M.

record.verdict_notes: Table 5 and Table 6 text is interleaved in the extraction; the reader took Table 5 Overall values for Table 6. The per-class means confirm Table 6 Overall as 47.8 / 71.5 / 78.3. The original sources are not this study. Uncertainty is not reported, and the losses are detection losses on auto-labels, not cross-entropy. The V5 verdict is limits_scope rather than challenges because loss does fall with scale; only the clean power-law form is disclaimed.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling for language models.
The paper does not test whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
It reports a qualitative compute-efficiency frontier, but does not fit or compare power-law growth rates for optimal model size and data size.
Width and depth are scaled together; the paper does not isolate architecture-shape effects at a fixed parameter count.
The study concerns supervised and auto-labeled 3D perception, not image or video generative models, repeated data, fine-tuning scaling laws, or transfer scaling laws generally.
It reports downstream detection performance after fine-tuning, but does not establish a predictive mapping from pretraining loss to downstream performance.
It does not systematically vary fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions, or training schedules to compare fitted exponents.

rows.subject: STELLAR model-size sweep (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Varied transformer width, feed-forward ratio, and layer count; plotted final loss against parameter count.

conditions.value: Fixed within each curve; examples cited include 3.2M and 51.2M

rows.measure: Final pretraining loss versus parameter count
rows.value: Figure only; text says loss consistently decreases with model size, with the steepest curves on smaller datasets and progressively flatter curves on larger datasets.
rows.note: The paper says the curves show diminishing returns and do not exhibit the strong log-linear scaling trends often reported in LLM literature. The figure overlays log-linear fits, but numerical fit parameters are not reported.
rows.check: State is right. Loss falls with parameters at every dataset size, but the authors say the trend shows diminishing returns, unlike strong LLM log-linear laws. The figure is not readable as numbers, and no fit coefficients are given.

source_check.correct: V5: partial. V7: observed; model-scaling curves flatten as dataset size increases, and the authors attribute distorted scaling to fixed-size components outside the scaled backbone.
source_check.locator_found: Section 6.1, Figure 3 and Table 2; Section 6.1 continuation above Figure 3.
source_check.problem: The shared partial state fits V5 but understates the observed setup dependence and curvature named by V7.

rows.subject: STELLAR models (aggregate across model sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of training examples and plotted final loss.
rows.measure: Final pretraining loss versus training-example count
rows.value: Figure only; text says increasing training-example size monotonically reduces loss for all models, with diminishing returns as curves flatten.
rows.note: The authors state they do not observe the strong log-linear scaling laws often reported in LLM literature and attribute this partly to auto-label quality and redundancy in driving data.
rows.check: State is right. Loss falls monotonically with data, but the curves flatten, and the authors say they do not observe strong LLM-like log-linear laws.

source_check.correct: V5: partial. V7: observed; increasing data monotonically reduces loss, but curves flatten and strong LLM-like log-linear scaling is not observed. Auto-label quality and driving-data redundancy are proposed explanations.
source_check.problem: The shared partial state fits V5; the reported curvature directly exhibits V7.

rows.subject: STELLAR model and dataset-size sweeps (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss across FLOP budgets, model sizes, and fixed dataset sizes; identified an efficient frontier.
rows.measure: Pretraining loss versus total compute, and loss along the efficient frontier
rows.value: Figure only; text says higher FLOP budgets improve performance, the efficient frontier is dominated by the largest dataset, and a smaller model trained on more data is more effective than a larger model trained on little data at the compared budget.
rows.note: This is a qualitative allocation result; the paper does not report fitted optimal parameter-count or token-count power laws.
rows.check: Remove the V3 link. The figure gives a qualitative frontier with no fitted optimal N or D versus compute, so it cannot show the stable power-of-compute growth V3 names; for V3 the row would be cannot_determine. For V5 the loss-versus-compute fall is shown, but with the same diminishing-returns caveat.
